title: Too Fast, Too Confident, Too Digital?
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner synthesizes two lines of research — Ronconi and Mason's 2026 study on digital reading comprehension and Gavriel Salomon's classic 1984 work on Amount of Invested Mental Effort (AIME) — to explain why students read digital texts faster, feel more confident about their understanding, and yet comprehend less than when reading print. The core argument is that screens carry cultural associations of ease and speed (scrolling, swiping, gaming) that cue low-effort reading habits, triggering the 'shallowing hypothesis': habitual digital media use reshapes reading toward surface-level processing. Unlike cognitive overload (too much demand), the problem here is under-investment of mental effort because the medium feels easy. Metacognitive monitoring — the ability to notice confusion and slow down — is impaired under digital conditions, producing a Dunning-Kruger-style gap: students think they understood more than they did. Kirschner pushes back on the standard intervention (teach digital literacy strategies) and argues that for complex expository texts requiring deep comprehension, the simpler solution is simply to print them.
points: Ronconi and Mason (2026) found a clear sequence: digital reading led to less time on text, which caused poorer comprehension monitoring, which produced lower actual understanding — and higher confidence ratings, a dangerous combination.

Salomon's AIME construct explains the mechanism: learners invest different amounts of mental effort not based on the difficulty of the text but on their perception of the medium. Screens feel easy; print feels like school-level seriousness, signaling that effort is required.

The problem is not cognitive overload but cognitive under-investment: students glide through digital text without pausing, rereading, or testing themselves, mistaking reading fluency for genuine understanding.

Kirschner reframes the intervention question — rather than building digital metacognitive strategies (though these still matter), educators should first ask why students are reading this particular text digitally at all, and default to print for complex expository material.
The medium sends signals about what kind of mental activity is required; instruction should match medium to learning goal, not assume digital is universally preferable because it is modern.
quotes: When students read digitally, they read faster, became more overconfident, and understood less. This isn't a small educational detail. It's a flashing RED warning light.

Salomon introduced the idea of Amount of Invested Mental Effort, which he defined as the number of nonautomatic mental elaborations learners apply to material. In other words: not how much effort the task objectively demands, but how much effort the learner actually chooses to put in. And that distinction matters enormously.

Digital reading feels easier, and because it feels easier, students invest less effort reading it. They glide through the text, don't pause, don't reread, don't test themselves, and don't notice confusion. They mistake fluency for understanding; metacognition gone wrong.

Students reading digitally weren't only understanding less; they were also more confident that they'd understood what they had read. They suffer from a variation of the Dunning-Kruger effect and can be seen as the educational equivalent of driving faster in fog while believing visibility has improved.

Why are they reading this text digitally in the first place? This sounds almost too simple, and that's why it'll probably be ignored. In education, we have a habit of creating problems and then designing interventions to solve the problems we've created.

Screens are associated with scrolling, chatting, searching, watching, gaming, swiping, and grazing. Paper, by contrast, still carries a school-like seriousness. It says: sit down, slow down, this matters.

For sustained reading and understanding of complex material, especially for children and young adolescents still developing the metacognitive skills that they need for independent study, print may reduce unnecessary problems and invite more appropriate effort.
